CURRENT QUESTION AND OPTIONS:
Based on the provided chest X-ray images, which of the following statements accurately describes the findings and their implications in this clinical case?

A) The PA chest X-ray (Figure 1a) shows a large solitary nodule with cavitation behind the right hemidiaphragm, which suggests a high likelihood of active tuberculosis.
B) The lateral chest X-ray (Figure 1b) confirms the presence of a large solitary nodule in the anterior right upper lobe, which is consistent with a typical presentation of a hamartoma.
C) The PA chest X-ray (Figure 1a) demonstrates a solitary nodule with smooth margins behind the right hemidiaphragm, and the lateral view (Figure 1b) confirms it in the posterior right lower lobe, consistent with a pulmonary inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.
D) The PA chest X-ray (Figure 1a) reveals multiple nodules scattered throughout both lungs, indicating a possible metastatic process rather than a solitary lesion.
E) The lateral chest X-ray (Figure 1b) shows a nodule with irregular margins in the right middle lobe, which aligns with the characteristics of a malignant neoplasm.
F) The PA chest X-ray (Figure 1a) demonstrates a calcified nodule behind the right hemidiaphragm, which is consistent with granuloma.

parent_passage.text:
When encountering indeterminate solid nodules on chest radiograph, ACCP guidelines
recommend thin-section chest CT as the next step unless prior imaging is available to prove
stability over 2 years (grade 1C recommendation) [2]. The purpose is to better characterize the
nodule and asses its malignant potential. To our knowledge, there is no relevant literature
describing effective ways to discriminate between benign and malignant nodules on radiographs
[2].
Variant 2: Adult greater than or equal to 35 years of age. Incidentally detected
indeterminate pulmonary nodule less than 6 mm on chest CT. Next imaging study.

Variant 2: Adult greater than or equal to 35 years of age. Incidentally detected
indeterminate pulmonary nodule less than 6 mm on chest CT. Next imaging study.
A. CT Chest Without IV Contrast
For incidental indeterminate pulmonary nodules measuring <6 mm on chest CT, Fleischner Society
guidelines do not recommend routine follow-up given the likelihood of malignancy is <1%. There
are exceptions for nodules with suspicious imaging features that increase the malignancy risk to
the 1% to 5% range. These features are described in Appendix 1. In those cases, a follow-up chest
CT may be appropriate at different time intervals, which are based on nodule attenuation, after
considering a patient’s preferences and comorbidities [9].
